3 adversarial vectors I constructed: (A) the real stale EZEK-P0-CURE-toolkit claim WITHOUT any supersession record - correctly REFUSED with 5 concrete reasons (missing sibling_sweep, 3-way digest mismatch); (B) the same stale claim made INTERNALLY self-consistent (verification/distinct_checker digests forged to match the stale claimed digest rather than the live file) - still correctly REFUSED, because every check compares against the LIVE on-disk digest, not internal consistency; (C) a supersession record present but carrying an unrelated/wrong old_artifact_sha256 - the record still retires the claim to SUPERSEDED, exposing a real (if minor) gap: see new_findings T3-01
cure_gate.result: Does a .md claim without sibling_sweep get refused? Yes (selftest + code read of check_claim's R6 branch). Does the supersession record retire EZEK-P0-CURE-toolkit? Yes, confirmed on the real claims file. Is a malformed supersession record refused? Yes (selftest vector, and the SUPERSESSION_KEYS presence check in run()). Can any path let a stale, unsuperseded claim read ACCEPTED? No such path was found: two independent adversarial attempts (a bare stale claim, and one forged for internal self-consistency) both correctly REFUSED, because claimed/verification/distinct_checker digests are always compared against the artifact's LIVE on-disk bytes, never against each other alone. One real but narrow gap was found and is recorded as new_finding T3-01: the supersession path itself does not authenticate old_artifact_sha256 or ordered_by against reality, so a well-formed but false supersession record can retire any cure_id to SUPERSEDED (a non-blocking, non-ACCEPTED status) undetected by this tool alone.

new_findings.claim: The R5 supersession-retirement path checks only that a supersession record carries the four required KEYS (supersedes_cure_id, recorded, ordered_by, why); it does not verify that old_artifact_sha256 matches the claim it purports to retire, nor that ordered_by names a ruling that actually exists. A well-formed but factually false supersession record therefore retires any named cure_id to SUPERSEDED - a non-ACCEPTED, non-blocking status - without any check on the record's truthfulness.
new_findings.evidence: Adversarial vector: the real EZEK-P0-CURE-toolkit claim paired with a hand-authored supersession record naming an unrelated old_artifact_sha256 ('f'*64, matching nothing) and ordered_by='test-adversarial' - the claim still read SUPERSEDED with refused:0, identical in shape to the genuine retirement.
new_findings.how_verified: Direct execution of _cure_verification.py --claims against a private adversarial fixture, compared to the genuine claims file's output.
new_findings.suggested_fix: Require old_artifact_sha256 in a supersession record to match the artifact_sha256 actually recorded on the claim it supersedes (cross-check against the claims already parsed from the same file), and/or require ordered_by to name a ruling id that a caller can optionally cross-verify against the controlling-rulings file. Low priority: this does not let anything read ACCEPTED, and R5's own authorization model (a controlling-agent ruling) is presumably enforced upstream of this tool, not by it - but the gap is worth disclosing since OW-10 exists specifically to prevent unverified self-reported closure.
